newsitem.title: UK: Show compassion, UK's Major urges Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Show compassion, UK's Major urges Conservatives.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major urged his Conservative party on Wednesday to show its compassionate side at the coming election, which he called a watershed for Britain.

In a pep talk to party activists in Huddersfield, a mainly working class town in northern England, Major said Britain now had the best-performing economy in Europe thanks to the free-market policies pushed through during the last 18 years of Conservative rule.
These achievements would be at risk if the main opposition Labour party confirmed opinion poll predictions and won the May 1 election, he said.
But Major said the ruling party had to reach out to those who had not yet benefited from the increased opportunities in education, health and ownership that the Conservatives had made possible.
"I don't think the Conservative party should be ashamed to show its compassionate side as well," the prime minister said.
The ruling party was not just for the well-heeled but for all those who shared its instincts. "We are an inclusive party and we need to make that more widely known," he said.

Declaring himself to be a "child of the welfare state", Major said he wanted another term in office to take advantage of the opportunities afforded by the robust health of the economy to tackle outstanding social problems.
"Give us the majority to complete the job we have set out to do," he urged.

Major said the strength of the economy made this a watershed election. "The prime minister and government on May 2, 1997, will inherit the best economy of any incoming government for 70 years," he said.

The Conservatives are about 25 percentage points behind Labour in the polls, and Major showed his frustration that his government has not reaped the credit for falling unemployment and quickening growth.
He said he wished everyone in Britain would recognise, as foreigners recognised, the advances Britain had made.
The quality of life had improved immeasurably and no capital in the world could match the artistic output of London, the prime minister argued. "We are a living success story," he said.
Labour, untested in office since 1979, would put those achievements at risk, Major said.
He kept up the attack on Blair's plans to give trade unions more rights, calling Labour "the financial subsidiary of the trade union movement."
Major's relaxed performance delighted the party faithful, who reserved their biggest cheer for his promise not to be dragged down the road to a European super-state.
Blair, by contrast, has said he would not allow himself to be isolated in Europe.
